questions.q: Using the method 'Government and the Ruler's Duties', work with: palana = 80, raksha = 10, yogakshema = 300. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of duties.
Take the relation taught for 'Government and the Ruler's Duties' and work with: palana = 150, raksha = 12, yogakshema = 30. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of duties.
Explain in your own words what 'Government and the Ruler's Duties' refers to.
questions.a: Government is the machinery that rules a country on the people's behalf; Kautilya sums a ruler's internal duties as three-fold, raksha or protection from aggression, palana or law and order within, and yogakshema or the welfare of the people.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Government and the Ruler's Duties'.
questions.a: Whoever rules is answerable for safety, order and welfare; types of government differ in who checks that answer.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Government and the Ruler's Duties', in plain ASCII form.
Explain in your own words what 'Democracy: Direct and Representative' refers to.
questions.a: In a democracy the people are the source of power: direct democracy lets all citizens decide together, while representative democracy, India's model, elects law-makers who answer to voters at fixed intervals.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Democracy: Direct and Representative'.
questions.a: Democracy turns rulers into servants: power is lent by the people and recalled at the ballot box.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Democracy: Direct and Representative' taught, and from which source text?

concepts.title: Monarchy and Other Forms of Rule

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Monarchy and Other Forms of Rule' refers to.
questions.a: In a monarchy rule passes by birth within a royal family, and the ruler is not elected; the chapter studies a different kind of monarchy too, where the king's power is checked by custom and counsel.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Monarchy and Other Forms of Rule'.
questions.a: Monarchy bets on birth, democracy on ballots; history shows both can rule well or badly, but only one answers to the people.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Monarchy and Other Forms of Rule' taught, and from which source text?
Explain in your own words what 'Who Checks the Rulers' refers to.
questions.a: Every form of government needs a check: democracies use constitutions and elections, even monarchies leaned on dharma and counsellors; where no check exists, the ruled have no remedy against misrule.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Who Checks the Rulers'.
questions.a: Power without accountability decays: the health of any government lies in what can question it.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Who Checks the Rulers' taught, and from which source text?
